items.stem: Outline the aim and method of Asch (1951).
items.answer: Aim: to investigate whether people conform to a clearly wrong majority judgement. Method: 123 male American college students judged line lengths in groups where all other members were confederates who gave the same wrong answer on 12 of 18 critical trials.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for an accurate aim (to investigate whether people conform to a clearly wrong majority judgement); 1 mark for an accurate method or design (123 male American college students judged line lengths in groups where all other members were confederates who gave the same wrong answer on 12 of 18 critical trials.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the biological approach and the cognitive approach.
items.answer: The biological approach explains behaviour through physical structures and processes (neurons, hormones, genes), while the cognitive approach explains it through information processing (attention, memory, thinking), often without specifying the neural basis.
items.markingKey: The biological approach explains behaviour through physical structures and processes (neurons, hormones, genes), while the cognitive approach explains it through information processing (attention, memory, thinking), often without specifying the neural basis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in Asch (1951), and explain how the dependent variable was operationalised.
items.answer: IV: presence of a unanimous majority giving wrong answers (vs control). DV: percentage of critical trials on which the participant gave the wrong answer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark IV (presence of a unanimous majority giving wrong answers (vs control)); 1 mark DV (percentage of critical trials on which the participant gave the wrong answer); 1 mark for an appropriate operationalisation or a relevant extraneous variable (e.g. participant variables, demand characteristics, order effects) with a brief justification.

items.stem: With reference to Asch (1951), explain how research has investigated the influence of the group on individual behaviour.
items.answer: Asch (1951). Aim: to investigate whether people conform to a clearly wrong majority judgement. Method: 123 male American college students judged line lengths in groups where all other members were confederates who gave the same wrong answer on 12 of 18 critical trials. Findings: participants conformed on about 37% of critical trials; about 75% conformed at least once; in a control condition errors were under 1% Link: the influence of the group on individual behaviour.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: participants conformed on about 37% of critical trials; about 75% conformed at least once; in a control condition errors were under 1%); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the influence of the group on individual behaviour. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Evaluate Asch (1951).
items.answer: Strengths: high control and a clear, objective task; control condition shows errors were due to social pressure. Limitations: all-male American students in the 1950s (cultural and historical bias); artificial task with low consequences; deception and distress.
items.markingKey: Strengths: high control and a clear, objective task; control condition shows errors were due to social pressure. Limitations: all-male American students in the 1950s (cultural and historical bias); artificial task with low consequences; deception and distress. Cultural consideration: Bond and Smith (1996) found higher conformity in collectivist cultures in their meta-analysis of 133 Asch-type studies. Award marks for points explicitly applied to this study (generic points score at most 1). items.stem: Which of the following was the aim of the study by Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997) on brain activity in murderers?
options: To measure how quickly learned information is forgotten over time
To test whether psychiatrists could reliably distinguish sane from insane people
To investigate whether people who had committed murder showed differences in brain functioning
To investigate whether people conform to a clearly wrong majority judgement
items.answer: To investigate whether people who had committed murder showed differences in brain functioning
items.markingKey: C. Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997) aimed to investigate whether people who had committed murder showed differences in brain functioning.

items.stem: Outline the findings of Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997) and explain one conclusion about the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: the murderers showed lower glucose metabolism in the prefrontal cortex and abnormal asymmetry in the amygdala and other limbic areas. Link: these results are evidence about the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (the murderers showed lower glucose metabolism in the prefrontal cortex and abnormal asymmetry in the amygdala and other limbic areas); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour (not just restating them).

items.stem: With reference to Ebbinghaus (1885), explain how research has investigated the scientific study of cognitive processes.
items.answer: Ebbinghaus (1885). Aim: to measure how quickly learned information is forgotten over time. Method: Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables (e.g. "WID") himself, then measured how much re-learning time was saved at intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days (the savings method). Findings: forgetting was rapid at first - over half was lost within the first hour or so - and then levelled off (the forgetting curve) Link: the scientific study of cognitive processes.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: forgetting was rapid at first - over half was lost within the first hour or so - and then levelled off (the forgetting curve)); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the scientific study of cognitive processes. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Explain one ethical consideration that is relevant to Asch (1951).
items.answer: Deception about the aim and the confederates, and stress from disagreeing with the group; participants were debriefed but could not give fully informed consent.
items.markingKey: Deception about the aim and the confederates, and stress from disagreeing with the group; participants were debriefed but could not give fully informed consent. 1 mark for identifying the issue; further marks for explaining it in the context of this study and (for discuss) how it was or could be addressed.

items.stem: Using one behaviour of your choice, explain how it could be studied from the biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches, and evaluate the benefit of combining them.
items.answer: Choose a behaviour (e.g. stress, aggression); give a specific explanation and study at each level (e.g. Kiecolt-Glaser et al. 1984; appraisal; social support); evaluate: combining gives a fuller, less reductionist account but is harder to test and may lack parsimony.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bias"?
options: The approach that explains behaviour in terms of mental processes such as perception, memory, thinking and decision-making
A systematic distortion in thinking, research design, measurement or interpretation that leads to inaccurate conclusions
The influence of the researcher's expectations or beliefs on how a study is designed, conducted or interpreted
The approach that explains behaviour in terms of the influence of other people, groups and culture
items.answer: A systematic distortion in thinking, research design, measurement or interpretation that leads to inaccurate conclusions
items.markingKey: B. "bias" is a systematic distortion in thinking, research design, measurement or interpretation that leads to inaccurate conclusions.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Responsibility is only relevant to researchers who use deception.
Reason (R): Researchers must consider the social consequences of their findings.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false - responsibility applies to all research; R is true.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why perspective matters when interpreting research findings.
items.answer: Researchers bring theoretical and cultural assumptions: a biological perspective may interpret depression as a neurochemical imbalance while a sociocultural one stresses poverty; WEIRD researchers may treat Western norms as universal (imposed etic). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Researchers bring theoretical and cultural assumptions: a biological perspective may interpret depression as a neurochemical imbalance while a sociocultural one stresses poverty; WEIRD researchers may treat Western norms as universal (imposed etic). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Discuss one ethical issue raised by the research of Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) and how it could be addressed.
items.answer: Teachers were deceived and some pupils may have received less attention; the potential harm to the control group raises questions of justice and protection from harm.
items.markingKey: Teachers were deceived and some pupils may have received less attention; the potential harm to the control group raises questions of justice and protection from harm. 1 mark for identifying the issue; further marks for explaining it in the context of this study and (for discuss) how it was or could be addressed.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Pygmalion effect in classrooms shows bias.
items.answer: Teachers in a California elementary school were told (falsely) that some randomly chosen pupils were "intellectual bloomers"; a year later those pupils showed larger IQ gains, especially in the youngest grades. Teachers' expectations, not pupils' ability, systematically changed outcomes - an expectancy (researcher/teacher) bias
items.markingKey: Context (Teachers in a California elementary school were told (falsely) that some randomly chosen pupils were "intellectual bloomers"; a year later those pupils showed larger IQ gains, especially in the youngest grades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: teachers' expectations, not pupils' ability, systematically changed outcomes - an expectancy (researcher/teacher) bias – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bias.

items.stem: With reference to Orne (1962), explain how research has investigated demand characteristics as a source of participant bias.
items.answer: Orne (1962). Aim: to show that participants actively try to work out and conform to the purpose of an experiment. Method: Participants were asked to add rows of random numbers on sheets, then tear each completed sheet into pieces and start again; Orne also compared "hypnotised" participants with those simulating hypnosis. Findings: participants persisted for hours at a meaningless task, interpreting it as an endurance test, showing that the experimental setting itself shapes behaviour Link: demand characteristics as a source of participant bias.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: participants persisted for hours at a meaningless task, interpreting it as an endurance test, showing that the experimental setting itself shapes behaviour); up to 3 marks for explicitly linking the findings to demand characteristics as a source of participant bias. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Evaluate the research by Rosenhan (1973) on the reliability of psychiatric diagnosis.
items.answer: Strengths: high ecological validity - real hospitals and staff; challenged diagnostic practice and influenced later manuals. Limitations: deception of hospital staff without consent; the accuracy of Rosenhan's account has since been questioned (Cahalan, 2019); claimed symptoms were real reports, so admission was arguably reasonable.
items.markingKey: Strengths: high ecological validity - real hospitals and staff; challenged diagnostic practice and influenced later manuals. Limitations: deception of hospital staff without consent; the accuracy of Rosenhan's account has since been questioned (Cahalan, 2019); claimed symptoms were real reports, so admission was arguably reasonable. items.stem: "Bias can never be fully removed from psychological research." Evaluate this claim with reference to research.
items.answer: Bias cannot be eliminated entirely, but well-designed, replicated and reflexive research can reduce it to the point where conclusions are credible.
items.markingKey: For: researchers are humans with expectations (Rosenthal); participants react to being studied; cultural assumptions shape questions. Against: double-blind procedures and standardisation greatly reduce bias; replication and peer review correct biased findings; triangulation and reflexivity make bias visible. items.stem: Explain how the concept of change applies to psychological theories.
items.answer: Theories are revised when new evidence appears - e.g. the multi-store model's single STM store was replaced by Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) working memory model; neuroplasticity research changed the view that the adult brain is fixed.

items.stem: Distinguish between correlation and causality.
items.answer: Causality means one variable produces a change in another (established by manipulating an IV under control); correlation only shows that two variables co-vary, which may be due to a third variable or reverse causation.

items.stem: A researcher in Hanoi uses a depression questionnaire developed in the USA. Identify one concept that is raised and explain the problem.
items.answer: Measurement/bias (also perspective): items may not have equivalent meaning in Vietnamese culture (e.g. somatic expression of distress), so the questionnaire may under- or over-estimate depression - an imposed etic.

items.stem: Explain one ethical consideration that is relevant to Rosenhan (1973).
items.answer: Hospital staff were deceived and observed without consent; the study could have damaged trust in psychiatric care.

items.stem: Using Rosenhan (1973) as supporting evidence, explain the reliability of measurement in psychiatric diagnosis.
items.answer: Rosenhan (1973). Aim: to test whether psychiatrists could reliably distinguish sane from insane people. Method: Eight healthy pseudo-patients reported hearing voices ("empty", "hollow", "thud") to gain admission to 12 US psychiatric hospitals, then behaved normally. Findings: all were admitted, seven with a diagnosis of schizophrenia; they stayed 7-52 days (mean 19) and were discharged "in remission"; other patients often detected them but staff did not Link: the reliability of measurement in psychiatric diagnosis.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: all were admitted, seven with a diagnosis of schizophrenia; they stayed 7-52 days (mean 19) and were discharged "in remission"; other patients often detected them but staff did not); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the reliability of measurement in psychiatric diagnosis. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the study by Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) provides convincing evidence about expectancy bias (the Pygmalion effect).
items.answer: Strengths: field setting gives high ecological validity; random selection of "bloomers" supports a causal conclusion. Limitations: effects were mainly in the youngest grades and later replications were mixed; ethical problems: deception of teachers and possible harm to control pupils; IQ test reliability for young children was questioned.
items.markingKey: Strengths: field setting gives high ecological validity; random selection of "bloomers" supports a causal conclusion. items.stem: Which model proposes that a disorder results from a vulnerability triggered by stress?
options: The social exchange model
The diathesis-stress model
The two-factor model
The multi-store model
items.answer: The diathesis-stress model
items.markingKey: B. Diathesis = vulnerability, stress = trigger.

items.stem: "If a behaviour is partly genetic, the environment cannot change it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Genes interact with the environment: Caspi et al. (2003) found the 5-HTT short allele increased depression risk only after stressful life events; environmental change can alter outcomes.
items.markingKey: Genes interact with the environment: Caspi et al. (2003) found the 5-HTT short allele increased depression risk only after stressful life events; environmental change can alter outcomes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the environment can change the expression of genes.
items.answer: Through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation: e.g. Weaver et al. (2004) showed that rat pups licked more by their mothers had altered methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene and lower stress responses.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation: e.g. Weaver et al. items.stem: Using an adolescent in Seoul who develops depression after academic failure as an example, explain the diathesis-stress model.
items.answer: Ji-ho, 17, has a family history of depression. After failing an entrance exam in a highly competitive system, he withdraws and blames himself. A genetic/cognitive vulnerability (family history, self-blaming style) interacts with a sociocultural stressor (exam pressure and stigma of failure) to trigger depression
items.markingKey: Context (Ji-ho, 17, has a family history of depression. After failing an entrance exam in a highly competitive system, he withdraws and blames himself.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Genes determine behaviour."
items.answer: Genes influence predispositions but do not determine behaviour; outcomes depend on gene-environment interaction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: twin studies show significant heritability (Kendler et al., 2006: about 38% for depression); specific gene variants are linked to behaviour. Arguments against: heritability is never 100%; environment explains much variance; gene effects depend on environment (Caspi et al., 2003); epigenetics shows environment changes gene expression. Supported judgement: Genes influence predispositions but do not determine behaviour; outcomes depend on gene-environment interaction.

items.stem: Which research method best describes the study by Dutton and Aron (1974) on arousal and attraction on a suspension bridge?

ethnographic participant observation
field experiment
covert participant observation
items.answer: field experiment

items.stem: Outline the findings of Dutton and Aron (1974) and explain one conclusion about the interaction of biological arousal and cognitive appraisal in emotion that can be drawn from them.

items.stem: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968), and explain how the dependent variable was operationalised.
items.answer: IV: whether teachers were told a pupil was a "bloomer". DV: gain in IQ test score over the year.

items.stem: With reference to Caspi et al. (2003), explain how research has investigated gene-environment interaction.
items.answer: Caspi et al. (2003). Aim: to investigate whether the 5-HTT gene moderates the effect of stressful life events on depression. Method: A longitudinal study of 847 New Zealanders from the Dunedin birth cohort, assessed for 5-HTT genotype, stressful life events between 21 and 26, and depression at 26. Findings: participants with one or two short alleles of 5-HTT showed more depression after stressful life events than those with two long alleles; genotype alone did not predict depression Link: gene-environment interaction.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: participants with one or two short alleles of 5-HTT showed more depression after stressful life events than those with two long alleles; genotype alone did not predict depression); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to gene-environment interaction. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Briefly describe a teenager in Mumbai who becomes anxious before exams and explain what it reveals about the three approaches to behaviour.
items.answer: Priya, 16, studies in Mumbai. Before exams her heart races and she cannot sleep; she believes she will fail and disappoint her family, whose expectations are high. Biological: activation of the HPA axis and cortisol release; cognitive: negative appraisal and catastrophising ("I will fail"); sociocultural: family expectations and a competitive, collectivist exam culture - each approach explains a different part of the anxiety
items.markingKey: Context (Priya, 16, studies in Mumbai. items.stem: With reference to Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968), explain how research has investigated expectancy bias (the Pygmalion effect).
items.answer: Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968). Aim: to investigate whether teachers' expectations can affect pupils' intellectual development. Method: Pupils at a California elementary school took an IQ test; teachers were told about 20% (randomly chosen) were "bloomers" expected to make big gains. Pupils were retested after 8 months and a year. Findings: the "bloomers" gained significantly more IQ points than controls, particularly in first and second grade Link: expectancy bias (the Pygmalion effect).
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: the "bloomers" gained significantly more IQ points than controls, particularly in first and second grade); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to expectancy bias (the Pygmalion effect). A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Psychology is just common sense." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many findings contradict common sense - e.g. Milgram (1963) found 65% of participants obeyed to 450 V, while psychiatrists predicted about 0.1% would; systematic research is needed because intuition is biased.

items.stem: A student claims: "Using a standardised questionnaire removes all bias from measurement." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Questionnaires can still be biased by social desirability, acquiescence, translation problems and culturally loaded items; standardisation improves reliability, not necessarily validity.
items.markingKey: Questionnaires can still be biased by social desirability, acquiescence, translation problems and culturally loaded items; standardisation improves reliability, not necessarily validity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the study by Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997) provides convincing evidence about the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour.
items.answer: Strengths: objective measure of brain activity (PET); matched controls for age and sex. Limitations: correlational - brain differences may be a result rather than a cause; special sample (insanity pleas) - not generalisable to all violent offenders; reductionist; ignores social factors such as childhood abuse.

items.answer: Biological

items.stem: Distinguish between participant bias and researcher bias.
items.answer: Researcher bias comes from the investigator's expectations (e.g. how they score responses), whereas participant bias comes from participants changing behaviour because they are being studied (demand characteristics, social desirability).

items.stem: Describe the study by Rosenhan (1973) and explain what it shows about the reliability of measurement in psychiatric diagnosis.
items.answer: Rosenhan (1973). Aim: to test whether psychiatrists could reliably distinguish sane from insane people. Method: Eight healthy pseudo-patients reported hearing voices ("empty", "hollow", "thud") to gain admission to 12 US psychiatric hospitals, then behaved normally. Findings: all were admitted, seven with a diagnosis of schizophrenia; they stayed 7-52 days (mean 19) and were discharged "in remission"; other patients often detected them but staff did not Link: the reliability of measurement in psychiatric diagnosis.

items.stem: With reference to an adolescent in Seoul who develops depression after academic failure, explain how it illustrates the diathesis-stress model.
items.answer: Ji-ho, 17, has a family history of depression. After failing an entrance exam in a highly competitive system, he withdraws and blames himself. items.stem: With reference to Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997), explain how research has investigated the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour.
items.answer: Raine, Buchsbaum and LaCasse (1997). Aim: to investigate whether people who had committed murder showed differences in brain functioning. Method: PET scans of 41 people charged with murder who pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity were compared with 41 matched controls while they completed a continuous performance task. Findings: the murderers showed lower glucose metabolism in the prefrontal cortex and abnormal asymmetry in the amygdala and other limbic areas Link: the role of brain structure and function in violent behaviour.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Behaviour is best explained by a single approach."
items.answer: A single approach can be useful for a specific research question, but a full explanation usually needs interaction between levels.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: parsimony: a single level is easier to test; some behaviours have strong single causes (e.g. HM's amnesia after surgery). items.stem: Critically assess the view that genes determine behaviour. Consider at least one methodological and one ethical or cultural issue.
items.answer: Genes influence predispositions but do not determine behaviour; outcomes depend on gene-environment interaction.
items.markingKey: For: twin studies show significant heritability (Kendler et al., 2006: about 38% for depression); specific gene variants are linked to behaviour. Against: heritability is never 100%; environment explains much variance; gene effects depend on environment (Caspi et al., 2003); epigenetics shows environment changes gene expression. Supported conclusion: Genes influence predispositions but do not determine behaviour; outcomes depend on gene-environment interaction.
